title: White Noise
description: White Noise was published by Viking in 1985 and won the National Book Award. It is narrated by Jack Gladney, professor of Hitler studies at the College-on-the-Hill in the invented town of Blacksmith, and it is in three parts: 'Waves and Radiation', 'The Airborne Toxic Event' and 'Dylarama'. The Norton selection is the second part, in which a chemical spill sends a black cloud over the town and the Gladneys are evacuated. It is the novel that made DeLillo famous and that gave American fiction the phrase 'the airborne toxic event' as a name for the accidents of late-industrial life.
plot_or_argument: The 'Airborne Toxic Event' section is the novel's centre, and it works by refusing the apocalyptic register that its material invites. DeLillo describes the evacuation in the flat documentary tone of a local news report: the traffic, the radio bulletins that revise the name of the chemical and the nature of the exposure, the family's bickering in the car, the refugee camp's improvised routines. The comedy is inseparable from the horror - the town's disaster is administered by the same institutions that run its schools and its supermarkets - and that is DeLillo's argument about late-industrial America: catastrophe is not an interruption of ordinary life but one of its services. Jack's exposure connects the public event to his private obsession with death, and the section ends with the two scaled to each other: the cloud that everyone shares and the mass that only he carries. The famous 'airborne toxic event' is a phrase the novel gives to the radio, and its migrations - the authorities rename the chemical and the event as the situation develops - are a study in how institutions manage language in order to manage fear. When the section closes, nothing has been resolved and everything has been normalised, which is the novel's point about the American 1980s.
narrative_structure: The novel is in three parts and forty chapters; the Norton selection is Part Two, which runs from the sirens to the return home, and it moves in short scenes between the road, the camp and the family's conversation, with radio bulletins and public-address announcements set into the narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Flat declarative sentences and a deadpan present tense; dialogue in which characters repeat the phrases of television, advertising and the news; lists of consumer goods used as a formal device; brand names treated as a natural part of speech; and a narrator who reports the uncanny without surprise.
historical_context: Published by Viking in 1985 and awarded the National Book Award for Fiction in 1985. It appeared in the decade of Bhopal (1984) and Chernobyl (1986), and its chemical cloud belongs to that moment; the novel's campus setting draws on DeLillo's time at Bennington College, where he taught in the early 1980s. White Noise is generally taken as the book that brought the American postmodern novel into the academic canon, and its second part is the section most often anthologised.
literary_significance: White Noise is DeLillo's best-known novel and one of the defining American books of the 1980s; its National Book Award marked the academy's recognition of the novel of media saturation, its second part is the standard anthology excerpt, and the phrase 'airborne toxic event' has passed into general American usage as a name for the industrial accident nobody predicted.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Viking Press in New York in 1985; the National Book Award for Fiction, 1985; the Norton selection is Part II, 'The Airborne Toxic Event'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the media's mediation of catastrophe: the radio names the event before anyone sees it, and the naming changes as the danger is reassessed, so that the language is a second disaster running alongside the first. The second is death, which the novel treats as a consumer problem - something to be feared, dosed, studied and sold. The third is the suburb as a system of consumption and waste, its supermarkets and its household products as the medium in which the family lives. The fourth is technology's ordinary violence, which the novel presents not as a takeover by machines but as the accidents of a system nobody is really running.
summary: Part One establishes the Gladney household - Jack, his fourth wife Babette, and the children from their earlier marriages - and its economy of consumption: the supermarket, the television, the radio, the family's talk about death. Jack has built a career on Hitler studies without speaking German; Babette teaches a course in posture and takes part in secret experiments. Part Two, the Norton selection, begins with the sirens: a tank car has derailed and released a cloud of Nyodene Derivative, and the town is evacuated to a Boy Scout camp in a slow, comic, terrifying procession of cars. Jack is exposed to the cloud while filling his car, and a technician later tells him he has a 'mass' of Nyodene in his body. The part ends with the family returned to a town whose normality has been revealed as a fiction. Part Three follows Jack's discovery that Babette has been taking an experimental drug, Dylar, that is supposed to abolish the fear of death, and his attempt to obtain it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the novel as the founding American text on media and simulation, and the 'Airborne Toxic Event' as its demonstration that the disaster is inseparable from its reporting; the family's 'toxic' consumer life, the Hitler studies satire and the Dylar plot have each produced substantial literatures, and the novel is regularly paired with Baudrillard and with the systems fiction of Pynchon.
research_notes: The novel is recorded as one work with the Norton excerpt noted in the bibliography statement, following the convention set for other excerpts. The book was not read in a copy of the first edition for this record; the plot is recorded from the critical and reference sources read.

title: Entropy
description: 'Entropy' was first published in The Kenyon Review for Spring 1960, when Pynchon was twenty-two and still at Cornell, and was collected in Slow Learner (1984). It is set in two adjacent apartments and moves between two parties: a rooftop gathering in a leaky Washington apartment building, and a sealed room on the floor below where a man named Callisto lives with his lover in a self-imposed bubble. The story takes the second law of thermodynamics as its governing metaphor and applies it to a culture.
plot_or_argument: 'Entropy' is a story built on a single scientific metaphor, and its interest is in how literally Pynchon takes it. Callisto's sealed apartment is an experiment in achieving equilibrium - the condition in which no further change is possible - and it is also a satire of the intellectual who withdraws from history into a constructed system. Meatball's party is the opposite: a mess of noise, alcohol and bodies that cannot be sealed. The story sets the two against each other and lets the second invade the first, which is the comic turn: entropy wins, but not in the way Callisto predicted. The prose is already the prose of the novels - long sentences, technical vocabulary used casually, jokes that depend on knowing what a Lagrangian is - and the two settings are the two poles of Pynchon's whole career: the engineered system and the uncontrollable crowd. It is an apprentice work, and Pynchon said so in the introduction he wrote for Slow Learner twenty-four years later, calling it 'a good deal of baloney' and an example of 'the kind of writing I was doing then'; but it is the seed of everything he wrote afterwards.
narrative_structure: A short story of about twenty pages that alternates between two adjacent settings, the rooftop party and the sealed apartment, with a third strand in which a bird enters the ventilation system; the strands converge without fully joining.
meter_and_prosody: Long sentences with a technical and colloquial mix; dialogue among the party's guests in period slang; scientific vocabulary used without explanation; and a narrator who is amused by his own characters.
historical_context: Published in The Kenyon Review, Spring 1960, and collected in Slow Learner (1984), where Pynchon added the introduction that remains his most extended autobiographical statement. The story was written while he was at Cornell and before his Navy service and Boeing; the cold-war Washington setting and the thermodynamic conceit belong to the moment when American writers were beginning to use science as a structure of metaphor rather than as a subject.
literary_significance: 'Entropy' is the Pynchon story most often anthologised and the standard introduction to his work for students, because it contains in miniature the two settings - the engineered system and the uncontrolled crowd - that his novels elaborate. It is a standard text in courses on postmodern fiction and on the use of science in literature.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Kenyon Review, Spring 1960; collected in Slow Learner (Little, Brown, 1984). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is entropy - the second law of thermodynamics - used as a metaphor for culture, history and personal life, and taken seriously enough to generate a plot. The second is the sealed room, and the intellectual's desire to build a system that history cannot reach. The third is the party: the unsealed, noisy, bodily world that refuses equilibrium. The fourth is the relation between them, which the story stages as a physical pressure - the noise coming through the floor - rather than as an argument.
summary: The story opens with Meatball Mulligan's lease-breaking party on the fourth floor of a Washington apartment building in the early 1960s: sailors, girls, a jazz record, a refrigerator full of gin. Below, in a hermetically sealed apartment kept at a constant temperature, Callisto and Aubade live inside a structure of his own making, and Callisto explains to her his theory that the world is moving towards 'heat-death', the state in which all energy is evenly distributed and no work is possible. He has built an 'entropic' situation on purpose: a sealed room where nothing can happen. The story cuts between the two floors, and the party's noise begins to penetrate the sealed room as a bird trapped in the ventilation; the two worlds blur. It ends with Meatball deciding to bring a representative of the other tenants to the party, and with the party - the human world of noise and disorder - beginning to invade the sealed room.
critical_context: Criticism treats the story as the apprentice piece that establishes Pynchon's thermodynamic imagination, and reads Callisto as a satire of the system-builder that his later novels would make sympathetic; the story's relation to the New Wave science fiction of the 1960s and to Pynchon's own later dismissal of it in Slow Learner are both standard topics.
research_notes: The Kenyon Review issue and season are recorded from the several accounts of the story's publication; the story was not read in the original periodical for this record.

title: Cathedral
description: 'Cathedral' was first published in The Atlantic Monthly for September 1981, was collected in The Best American Short Stories 1982, and became the title story of Cathedral (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1983). It is narrated by a man whose wife has invited a blind friend, Robert, to stay the night, and it describes an evening in which the narrator's suspicion and condescension are undone by an act of shared drawing.
plot_or_argument: 'Cathedral' is the story in which Carver's later manner arrives, and its method is withholding. The narrator's voice is so complete - so full of unearned certainty - that the story can dispense with commentary; the reader hears the prejudice in his own words and is never told what to think about it. The ending is the only moment in the story where something happens that the narrator cannot describe, and that is exactly why it works: the man who has narrated everything with confidence is left with his eyes closed, and the story stops there rather than telling us what he understood. Carver said that in writing it he knew he had 'gone as far the other way as I could or wanted to go, cutting everything down to the marrow', and the story is the hinge between the severe minimalism of What We Talk About When We Talk About Love and the more expansive manner of his last books. The drawing scene - two men with their hands on a sheet of paper, one of them blind - is one of the best known endings in American short fiction, and its power comes from the fact that the story has spent twenty pages establishing how little the narrator could see.
narrative_structure: A single first-person narrative in the past tense, without scene breaks, covering one evening from the narrator's waiting for the visit to the final drawing; the ending is a single closing gesture rather than a resolution.
meter_and_prosody: Short sentences and a flat, colloquial first person; dialogue that reproduces ordinary speech including its repetitions and failures; very little metaphor; and an ending that withholds the character's realisation.
historical_context: Published in The Atlantic Monthly in September 1981 and collected in Cathedral (Knopf, 1983), which was nominated for the National Book Critics Circle Award and the Pulitzer Prize. Carver was in the last years of his life when the collection appeared, and the story's movement away from the severe cuts of Gordon Lish's editing of the previous book is part of its history; the unedited manuscripts published after Carver's death have changed how the story is read.
literary_significance: 'Cathedral' is probably the most anthologised American short story of the last forty years and the one most often used to teach the form; it is a set text in courses on American fiction and on the short story, and its ending is one of the standard examples of the contemporary epiphany.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Atlantic Monthly, September 1981; collected in The Best American Short Stories 1982 and in Cathedral (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1983). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is blindness, both literal and figurative, and the story is careful to let the literal blindness belong to the man who sees more. The second is class: the narrator's defensiveness is the defensiveness of a man without work, in a house his wife's salary sustains. The third is the ordinary American domestic evening - the television, the dinner, the drinks - used as the entire stage. The fourth is art, which arrives not as an object but as an act of shared attention, and which is the only thing in the story that the narrator cannot talk his way out of.
summary: The narrator, unemployed and at home in the American Northwest, tells the story of the visit in a flat, defensive voice: he has never met Robert, a blind man who worked with his wife years earlier and whose voice has been on tapes they have exchanged for a decade. The narrator's account is full of casual prejudice - he assumes the man will be dull, that his wife's former marriage was a mistake, that blindness is a kind of absence - and the story lets him expose himself without comment. Robert arrives, eats a large dinner, smokes, and watches television with the family. Late in the evening, with the wife asleep, a programme about cathedrals comes on, and the narrator cannot describe one. Robert asks him to draw one, then puts his hand over the narrator's as he draws, and the story ends with the narrator's eyes still closed, feeling the paper, 'with my eyes still closed'.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as the turning point in Carver's style and as an instance of what has been called his 'post-minimalist' manner; the role of Gordon Lish in shaping Carver's earlier stories has made the story central to the argument about editing and authorship, and its treatment of blindness has been discussed in disability studies as well as in formal criticism.
research_notes: The Atlantic Monthly printing of September 1981 is recorded from the critical and reference accounts read; some of those accounts give March 1981, and the discrepancy is noted here rather than resolved. The collection date of 1983 follows the Knopf first edition.

title: The Lesson
description: 'The Lesson' was published in Gorilla, My Love (New York: Random House, 1972), Toni Cade Bambara's first collection of stories. It is narrated by Sylvia, a girl of about nine, who is taken with her cousin and the other neighbourhood children by Miss Moore - the one woman on the block with a college degree - to a toy store on Fifth Avenue, and who works out for herself what the trip has been for.
plot_or_argument: 'The Lesson' is a story about the education of a child who refuses to be educated in public, and its entire effect depends on the gap between what Sylvia understands and what she will admit. Bambara's narrator is one of the great voices in American short fiction: the grammar, the invective, the fierce loyalty to her own world are all rendered without a trace of the author's correction. The trip to the toy store is a lesson in the price of things, and the story's achievement is that it makes the reader feel the arithmetic - a thousand-dollar boat in a shop a cab ride from a neighbourhood where children count coins - as Sylvia feels it, as an insult rather than a statistic. The ending is deliberate: Miss Moore does not get her answer, Sugar does not get her lesson, and Sylvia, who has learned the most, says nothing. That withholding is Bambara's politics - the education has happened, but it belongs to the child, not to the teacher - and it is why the story has become a standard text in courses on American fiction and on the teaching of class.
narrative_structure: A single first-person retrospective narrative in the voice of a child, moving from the assembling of the children through the cab ride and the toy store to the walk home; the story's climax is a conversation overheard rather than an event.
meter_and_prosody: First-person narration in Black vernacular, with the spelling and grammar rendered rather than corrected; heavy use of dialogue and of the narrator's commentary; comedy carried by invective; and an ending that withholds the narrator's conclusion.
historical_context: Published in Gorilla, My Love (Random House, 1972), Bambara's first collection, and set in the Harlem and Brooklyn of her own childhood. The story belongs to the Black Arts and Black feminist writing of the early 1970s, and to a moment when American short fiction was beginning to record the speech of Black neighbourhoods without translation.
literary_significance: 'The Lesson' is the most anthologised story Bambara wrote and one of the standard texts of the American short story of the 1970s; it is taught in courses on American fiction, on the literature of class and on Black women's writing, and its narrator's voice is regularly cited as a model of vernacular narration.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Gorilla, My Love (New York: Random House, 1972). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is class as it is learned by a child, through prices rather than through argument. The second is education and who controls it: Miss Moore is an outsider in her own neighbourhood because she has been to college, and the story is alive to the resentment that her benevolence provokes. The third is race and the city, since the distance between Harlem and Fifth Avenue is travelled in a cab and is a distance in history as much as in geography. The fourth is pride, which the story treats as a form of knowledge rather than as an obstacle to it.
summary: The story opens with Miss Moore assembling the children on a summer day - 'back in the days when everyone was old and stupid or young and foolish and me and Sugar were the only ones just right' - and Sylvia's resentment of her is established at once: the woman is 'black as hell' and has 'nappy hair' and no makeup and is always organising something educational. The trip takes them in two cabs to F. A. O. Schwarz, where the children look at a toy sailboat that costs more than a thousand dollars, a clown that costs thirty-five, and a paperweight with a tiny glass sculpture inside. Sylvia reads the price tag, is furious, and refuses to give Miss Moore the satisfaction of an answer. The story ends on the walk back: Sugar says that the country must be 'a democracy if you ask me, equal and fair', and then breaks away to spend her money; Sylvia, left alone, thinks that 'nobody gonna beat me at nuthin'.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a study of the pedagogy of class and as an instance of Bambara's vernacular method; the figure of Miss Moore has been discussed as a critique of middle-class uplift, and Sylvia's refusal to answer has been read as the story's own refusal to deliver a lesson to its reader.
research_notes: The collection, publisher and year are recorded from the catalogue and reference records read; the story was not read in a copy of the first edition for this record.

title: The Woman Warrior
description: The Woman Warrior: Memoirs of a Girlhood Among Ghosts was published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1976 and won the National Book Critics Circle Award for general nonfiction. It is in five parts - 'No Name Woman', 'White Tigers', 'Shaman', 'At the Western Palace' and 'A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe' - and it moves between the author's childhood in Stockton, California, her mother's talk-stories, and the Chinese legends her mother told. The Norton selection prints 'No Name Woman' and an excerpt from 'A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe'.
plot_or_argument: The Woman Warrior changed the American memoir by refusing to decide what kind of book it was. Its five parts are held together by the voice of the daughter and by the practice the book calls 'talk-story' - the Chinese American habit of telling a story that is not quite true in order to say something that is - and the book's most important formal decision is to leave the reader unable to tell which passages are remembered, which are invented and which are translated legend. 'No Name Woman', the section the Norton prints in full, is the clearest demonstration: the narrator gives three or four possible stories of her aunt and never chooses, and the refusal is the point, since the woman's history was erased and any single version would complete the erasure in a different way. Kingston's prose carries the cadence of her mother's speech into English, and the book's anger - at the village, at the family, at the American school system that kept her silent for years - is delivered without editorial comment. It is a founding text of Asian American literature, and it was also the centre of the decade's argument about authenticity, in which Frank Chin and others accused Kingston of falsifying Chinese tradition for a white readership. Both the book's formal originality and that argument are now part of its history.
narrative_structure: Five parts that can be read as essays, stories or chapters: 'No Name Woman', 'White Tigers', 'Shaman', 'At the Western Palace' and 'A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe'; the book's unity is carried by the narrating voice and by recurring images rather than by chronology.
meter_and_prosody: A first-person prose that keeps the rhythm of spoken Chinese-influenced English; direct address to the reader and to the dead; abrupt movement between legend, memory and commentary; and a refusal to mark which is which.
historical_context: Published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1976; 'No Name Woman' had appeared, in slightly different form, in Viva for January 1975, and the book's copyright page records that. It appeared in the decade of the Asian American movement and of the women's movement, and it was attacked from both directions - by Frank Chin and others for falsifying tradition, by some feminists for not being feminist enough - which is a measure of how directly it intervened in both arguments.
literary_significance: The Woman Warrior is the founding text of Asian American literary memoir and one of the most widely taught American books of the period; its National Book Critics Circle Award, its decade of controversy and its influence on the memoirs and novels that followed make it indispensable, and the Norton Anthology prints two sections of it.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York in 1976; 'No Name Woman' appeared in slightly different form in Viva, January 1975. The Norton selection prints 'No Name Woman' and an excerpt from 'A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the relation between a daughter and a mother whose stories are the daughter's only access to her history, and the book's method is to keep that relation unresolved. The second is silence: the girl who cannot speak in American classrooms, the aunt who is not spoken of, the women whose lives were not recorded. The third is migration and its erasures - the aunts left in China, the husbands who did not send for them, the paper identities of the exclusion era. The fourth is the making of a woman writer, which the book presents not as a triumph but as a series of refusals, ending with the daughter's song that is also her mother's.
summary: 'No Name Woman' opens with the mother's warning, delivered as the daughter begins to menstruate: she must not tell anyone what she is about to be told. The story is of an aunt in China who became pregnant by a man the village never identified, gave birth alone in a pigsty after the village raided the house, and drowned herself and the baby in the family well; the family has since behaved as if she never existed. The narrator reconstructs the aunt's story from the fragments her mother gave her, offering several incompatible explanations - rape, seduction, love - and refusing to settle on one. 'White Tigers' recounts the legend of Fa Mu Lan, the woman warrior, and the narrator's childhood training in it. 'Shaman' tells of her mother's medical training in China and the ghosts she encountered there. 'At the Western Palace' concerns an aunt who came to America and found her husband had taken another wife. 'A Song for a Barbarian Reed Pipe' is about the narrator's own girlhood, her silence in American schools, and her final breaking of that silence against her mother.
critical_context: Criticism treats the book as the central case in the argument over Asian American representation, as an experiment in genre that anticipated the mixed-form memoir of the 1980s and 1990s, and as a feminist text about silence and voice; the Chin-Kingston dispute is documented in Asian American literary history and is still taught as a debate about who owns a tradition.
research_notes: The book is recorded once for both of its Norton selections, following the convention set for excerpts. The copyright page gives the Viva printing of January 1975; the first edition was not read for this record.

title: Lullaby
description: 'Lullaby' was first published in Laguna Woman (1974), Leslie Marmon Silko's first book, a collection of poems and stories, and was collected in Storyteller (1981). It is set in the winter of the 1970s in the American Southwest and concerns an old Navajo woman, Ayah, and her husband Chato, and the losses that have accumulated over their marriage.
plot_or_argument: 'Lullaby' is a story of accumulated dispossession told without a single accusatory sentence, and its restraint is what makes it unbearable. Silko gives the facts - the children taken, the land lost, the husband dying - in the order in which Ayah remembers them rather than in chronological order, so that the reader assembles the history at the same time as the character relives it. The white men who took the children are described only as they appeared to a woman who did not understand their language, which both limits the reader's access to the scene and makes the scene's violence feel arbitrary, as it must have felt. The ending, in which Ayah lies down in the snow beside her dying husband and sings the lullaby, is one of the most famous in Native American fiction: it is not a surrender, because the song is an act of survival, carrying the language and the memory forward even as the body gives up. Silko's prose here is plain and unhurried, closer to the oral tradition she was raised in than to the contemporary short story, and that is the story's argument as well as its form.
narrative_structure: A single short story that moves between Ayah's present (the drive into the snow) and her recollections, without scene breaks or dates; the movement between them is associative and the story's chronology has to be assembled by the reader.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, unhurried third-person prose with almost no metaphor; dialogue rendered in Ayah's English and in Chato's; the landscape given in concrete physical detail; and an ending that resolves on an action rather than an explanation.
historical_context: First published in Laguna Woman (1974), Silko's first book, which collected poems and short stories and was a small-press production; the story reached a wide readership through Storyteller (1981), the mixed-form book in which Silko set her stories alongside photographs and poems. The removal of Native children to boarding schools and foster care was a live political issue throughout the 1970s, and the Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 was passed in the same years.
literary_significance: 'Lullaby' is one of the two or three most anthologised Native American short stories and the standard introduction to Silko's shorter work; it is taught in courses on Native American literature and on the American short story, and its ending is regularly cited as an example of how a story can hold grief and survival at once.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Laguna Woman (Greenfield Center, NY: Greenfield Review Press, 1974); collected in Storyteller (New York: Little, Brown, 1981). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the removal of Native children, which the story presents as the central violence of the twentieth century and records without editorialising. The second is land: the shack, the land that has gone out of the family's hands, the snow - all given as the substance of a life rather than as a setting. The third is language, since Ayah's Navajo is a world the English-speaking authorities cannot enter, and the lullaby at the end is the story's assertion that something survives. The fourth is marriage, and the story's unsentimental picture of a union made under pressure and held together by endurance.
summary: Ayah is old and blind in one eye and lives with Chato, a Mexican American who worked for years for the white ranchers, in a shack on land that has passed out of their hands. Their children have been taken from them: two died in infancy, one son was killed in the Korean War, and the others were taken by the authorities - the narrator remembers the day the white men came and took the children away while Chato was away. The story moves in Ayah's memory between these losses and the present, in which she and Chato are travelling towards the town in the snow; Chato drinks and then disappears into a storm, and Ayah goes to look for him. She finds him in the snow and lies down beside him, and the story closes with her singing a lullaby in Navajo, the song she sang to her infants, as she covers him and herself against the cold.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a study of child removal and of the survival of language, and discusses its circular structure as an instance of the oral tradition's influence on Silko's form; it is usually paired with 'Ceremony' and with the stories of Storyteller, and the Navajo lullaby at the end has been the focus of the considerable body of work on Silko and song.
research_notes: The first publication in Laguna Woman (1974) is recorded from the bibliographic records of Silko's work; the story was not read in a copy of that edition for this record.

title: Language and Literature from a Pueblo Indian Perspective
description: 'Language and Literature from a Pueblo Indian Perspective' is the text of a talk Silko gave at a conference at the State University of New York at Buffalo in 1979, published in the conference volume The First Words in 1981. It is the clearest statement she has given of how Pueblo storytelling works and of what happened to it when it met the written page, and it is the essay through which her poetics is most often taught.
plot_or_argument: The essay is a performance in prose, and its argument is carried by its own form: Silko refuses the conference paper's structure and demonstrates the Pueblo structure instead. The content is therefore inseparable from the way it is delivered - a point she makes explicit when she says that a Pueblo audience would already know the stories she is telling and would interrupt her, and that the non-Pueblo reader has to be told this, which is itself the subject of the essay. Her account of the oral tradition is precise rather than mystical: stories are not free-floating symbols but property, owned by families and clans, told at particular times, and their function is to keep the community's memory in working order. The essay's treatment of writing is generous and unsentimental - English is a language the Pueblo people have now, and the stories will change in it - and it closes with a story rather than a conclusion because a conclusion would be, in the essay's own terms, the wrong shape. It is the essay most often cited for the proposition that Native American literature is not a subject matter but a set of forms.
narrative_structure: A lecture that proceeds by anecdote and example rather than by argument, in numbered movements that correspond loosely to the parts of a Pueblo storytelling session, and closes with a story in place of a conclusion.
meter_and_prosody: Spoken, unhurried prose with direct address to the audience; short declarative sentences set against long narrative ones; no footnotes or citations; and a deliberate refusal of academic vocabulary.
historical_context: Delivered at a conference at the State University of New York at Buffalo in 1979 - the conference on Native American literature that also produced the volume The First Words (1981) - at a moment when Native American writers were beginning to define the field's terms for themselves. The essay is contemporaneous with Storyteller (1981) and shares that book's conviction that the oral tradition is a living form rather than a source.
literary_significance: 'Language and Literature from a Pueblo Indian Perspective' is the standard statement of Native American poetics by one of its central practitioners and is anthologised in the Norton Anthology, in collections of American essays and in course readers on Native American literature; it is the essay most often assigned alongside Momaday's The Way to Rainy Mountain and Silko's own fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The First Words: The Proceedings of a Conference on Native American Literature (1981) and collected in Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit: Essays on Native American Life Today (New York: Simon and Schuster, 1996). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the structure of oral narrative - the way stories nest inside one another, the role of the audience, the ownership of stories - described from inside rather than as anthropology. The second is translation and loss, treated without nostalgia and without celebration. The third is community: the essay insists that a story belongs to people, not to a literature. The fourth is survival, which the essay presents as a matter of continuing to tell the stories in whatever language is available.
summary: Silko begins by explaining that she will not give a conventional paper, because the Pueblo way of speaking does not proceed by thesis and argument; instead she tells stories, and lets the stories carry the argument. She describes the structure of a Pueblo narrative - the way one story opens into another, the way the teller must know where every part of the community's history connects - and the importance of the audience, who may interrupt and who know the stories already. She gives examples: the story of the Laguna migration, the story of the gambler, and the story of how the people came up from the underworld. She then addresses the movement of oral narrative into English and into print, the loss that accompanies translation, and the continuance of the stories in new forms. She closes by telling the audience a story rather than concluding.
critical_context: Criticism reads the essay as the founding statement of a Pueblo aesthetics in English, and discusses its formal refusal of the academic paper as itself an argument about what counts as theory; it is regularly paired with Momaday's essays and with the work of Paula Gunn Allen on the sacred in Native American literature.
research_notes: The Buffalo conference of 1979 and the 1981 volume are recorded from the accounts of the essay's publication; the exact conference title and the page numbers were not established from the sources consulted and are not stated above.

title: Neo-HooDoo Manifesto
description: 'Neo-HooDoo Manifesto' is the opening statement of Conjure: Selected Poems 1963-1970 (Amherst: University of Massachusetts Press, 1972), and it is Reed's declaration of an aesthetic: a Black American art built on hoodoo - the African-derived folk magic of the American South - rather than on the European tradition, written in a mixture of manifesto prose, verse, parody and joke.
plot_or_argument: 'Neo-HooDoo Manifesto' is one of the founding documents of the Black postmodern mode in American writing, and its strategy is to be a manifesto that makes fun of manifestos while making a real one. Reed's argument - that Black American culture has its own metaphysics, its own epistemology and its own procedures for making art, and that these are not decorative alternatives to the European tradition but its historical adversaries - is made in the form of a joke that keeps turning serious. The piece's typography and its switches of register are part of the argument: an aesthetic that cannot be contained in a paragraph of academic prose is expressed in a form that will not fit one. It belongs to the same moment as Mumbo Jumbo (1972), his novel of the Harlem Renaissance as a hoodoo conspiracy, and the two works together state the position that Reed has held for fifty years. It is a difficult text to anthologise precisely because it depends on performance, and its presence in the Norton selection is a measure of how central that difficulty has become to the American canon.
narrative_structure: A short, discontinuous text in sections of prose and verse that has no continuous argument and ends without a conclusion; its unity is carried by the voice and by recurring terms.
meter_and_prosody: A mixture of manifesto prose, verse, parody, catalogue and joke; deliberate self-contradiction; typographic play; a vocabulary drawn from hoodoo, the church, advertising and the academy; and a tone that is never entirely straight.
historical_context: Published at the head of Conjure: Selected Poems 1963-1970 (University of Massachusetts Press, 1972), at the height of Reed's involvement with the Black Arts Movement, and in the same year as Mumbo Jumbo. Reed's Neo-HooDoo aesthetic was developed across those two books and the Yardbird anthologies he edited from 1973, and it was offered as an alternative to both the Black Arts Movement's nationalism and the white avant-garde's experimentalism.
literary_significance: 'Neo-HooDoo Manifesto' is the statement of the aesthetic that made Reed the most consistently inventive Black American postmodernist and is a standard anthology text in courses on African American literature and on the American postmodern; its influence is visible in the fiction of Paul Beatty, Colson Whitehead and the writers of the twenty-first century who treat Black history as a store of forms to be recombined.
bibliographical_notes: Published at the head of Conjure: Selected Poems 1963-1970 (Amherst: University of Massachusetts Press, 1972). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the existence of an African-derived American aesthetics, argued as a matter of fact rather than as a claim for recognition. The second is the Western art institution, which the manifesto treats as a rival religion with its own priests. The third is parody as method: the manifesto's jokes are not decoration but argument, since a form that cannot be taken seriously by the academy is exactly the form Reed wants. The fourth is the reader, who is addressed as an audience at a performance and thereby made responsible for the piece's completion.
summary: The piece declares that 'Neo-HooDoo' is 'the special deity' of the American Black, and proceeds through definitions, lists and satirical routines: hoodoo is opposed to the 'Western aesthetic', to the museum, to the academy and to the idea of art as a separate realm. Reed names the practical sources - the conjure men, the church, the blues, the signifying tradition - and he attacks the institutions that have excluded Black art, including the publishing industry and the critics. The manifesto is deliberately self-contradictory: it asserts and denies in the same paragraph, uses the language of advertising and of the Old Testament interchangeably, and treats the reader as a participant in a performance rather than as a recipient of an argument.
critical_context: Criticism treats the manifesto as the founding text of Neo-HooDoo and reads it alongside Mumbo Jumbo as a single project; its relation to the Black Arts Movement, which Reed supported while refusing its orthodoxies, and to the postmodern novel's use of the archive are the standard topics.
research_notes: The volume, publisher and year are recorded from the catalogue records of Conjure; the piece was not read in a copy of that edition for this record.

title: Hunger of Memory
description: Hunger of Memory: The Education of Richard Rodriguez was published by David R. Godine in 1982. It is in six parts - a prologue, 'Aria', 'The Achievement of Desire', 'Credo', 'Complexion' and 'Profession' - and it is an autobiography of assimilation told as an argument against the politics of assimilation. The Norton selection prints an excerpt.
plot_or_argument: Hunger of Memory is a memoir that argues, and its argument is uncomfortable by design. Rodriguez presents his own success - Stanford, Columbia, a Berkeley PhD programme - as a series of losses, and he refuses the consolations that the genre of the immigrant autobiography normally supplies: there is no reconciliation with the family, no recovery of Spanish, no return to the community that made him. The book's most quoted sentence, that the scholarship boy 'cannot afford to think about himself', is a description of a class position as much as a psychological one. Its political intervention was to refuse the label of minority writer while claiming the experience of one, and to argue that bilingual education and affirmative action had, in his own case, cost more than they gave; those arguments made him famous and made him the target of sustained criticism from Mexican American writers. The prose is formal and deliberate, closer to the nineteenth-century essay than to the confessional memoir of the 1970s, and the book's design - six essays rather than a chronology - is itself an argument that a life is best understood as a set of propositions. The book's refusal to be grateful is what has kept it alive: it declines to turn its author's success into a story the reader can be comforted by, and it declines, equally, to apologise for it.
narrative_structure: A prologue and five chapters - 'Aria', 'The Achievement of Desire', 'Credo', 'Complexion' and 'Profession' - each an essay that can stand alone and that is ordered thematically rather than chronologically.
meter_and_prosody: Formal, periodic, essayistic prose with a strong first person; quotation and allusion used as evidence; a refusal of the confessional register; and endings that refuse the resolution the reader expects.
historical_context: Published by David R. Godine in Boston in 1982, at a moment when bilingual education and affirmative action were the central arguments of American racial politics, and when the Mexican American literary renaissance was producing its first major memoirs. The book's intervention in those arguments - from a position that was read as a rejection of the community it described - made it one of the most discussed American memoirs of the decade.
literary_significance: Hunger of Memory is one of the foundational American memoirs of the period and the book that made assimilation a public argument for a Mexican American writer; it is a standard text in courses on American autobiography, on Chicano literature and on the politics of education, and the debate it provoked remains part of the literature.
bibliographical_notes: First published by David R. Godine in Boston in 1982; the Norton selection is an excerpt. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is language and the private/public split, which the first chapter establishes as the book's founding loss. The second is education as a form of class migration and the guilt that accompanies it. The third is religion, which Rodriguez treats as a private structure of meaning rather than as a community. The fourth is race and colour within a family and a society, in the chapter on complexion. The fifth is the public argument about affirmative action and bilingual education, which the book intervenes in directly.
summary: 'Aria' describes the Rodriguez family's life in Sacramento in the 1950s, when the children spoke Spanish at home and English was a public language, and the day the nuns came to the house to ask the parents to speak English to their children; the chapter is about the silence that followed, and the loss of the family's intimate speech. 'The Achievement of Desire' is an account of his education, built around his reading of Richard Hoggart's The Uses of Literacy and his recognition of himself in the figure of the 'scholarship boy' who is educated away from his family. 'Credo' describes his Catholicism and his refusal of the communal, ritual church for a private faith. 'Complexion' concerns his dark skin and the shame it caused him and his family. 'Profession' describes his refusal of a professorship and his decision to write instead.
critical_context: Criticism reads the book as the central case in the argument over assimilation and as an instance of the essay sequence as autobiography; Mexican American and Chicano critics have attacked its politics while acknowledging its literary force, and the book is routinely paired with Gloria Anzaldúa's Borderlands as the two poles of Mexican American writing about language in the period.
research_notes: The book is recorded as one work with the Norton excerpt noted, following the convention set for excerpts. The first edition was not read for this record; the chapter titles are from the book's contents as recorded by the sources consulted.
